883.title: the crossing of the Yamuna
883.hook: on the far bank, a whole village is asleep, and Vasudeva has to leave his son beside a sleeping stranger
883.howItsDone: Hindus honor Yashoda as Krishna's foster mother, and Nanda's household in Gokula is remembered in songs and festivals of Krishna's childhood; Nandotsava, the celebration in Nanda's village, is kept by some communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday the guards slept, the doors opened, Shesha's hoods sheltered father and child, and the river gave way. Your line was the river gives way.

Gokula is silent. Vasudeva comes up out of the river, soaked, with the baby in his arms, and walks into the cowherd village where his friend Nanda lives. Nobody stops him. Nobody even stirs. The Bhagavata says everyone in Nanda's household is fast asleep. Inside, Nanda's wife Yashoda has just given birth too. She lies beside a newborn girl, so deeply asleep that she doesn't know what kind of child she has had.
screen: `GOKULA IS SILENT.` → `NANDA'S HOUSE ASLEEP.` → `YASHODA AND A NEWBORN GIRL.`

segments.voice: He makes the exchange. He lays his son down beside Yashoda and picks up her daughter. Then he walks back the way he came: across the river, through the open doors, into the prison. He sets the girl down on Devaki's bed. The text says he put the fetters back on his own feet, and the doors closed, as if nothing had happened. This is the man who walked into a flood to save his son, and his journey ends with giving that son away, to a woman who doesn't know, in a house where he can't stay, and walking himself back into chains. The rescue only works if he goes back. And there is the girl: someone else's newborn daughter, carried into the prison where Kamsa killed Devaki's children. The Bhagavata has told us who she is: Yogamaya, the Lord's own power, born to Yashoda for exactly this. Vasudeva may not fully know. He carries her anyway. And Yashoda will wake up to a son. In the stories ahead she is his mother in every way they show: the one who feeds him, chases him, scolds him, and ties him up when he steals butter. A crossing usually means reaching the other side and staying there. This one means leaving the most precious thing on the other side, and coming home with empty arms.

884.title: the crossing of the Yamuna
884.hook: a baby cries in the prison, Kamsa comes running, and the child he reaches for slips out of his hands into the sky
884.carry: stop killing the helpless for nothing
884.howItsDone: Hindus who follow the Bhagavata honor the girl born to Yashoda as Yogamaya, a form of the Goddess, and in some places she is worshiped as a sister of Krishna.

segments.voice: Yesterday Vasudeva left his son beside sleeping Yashoda and carried her daughter back into the prison. Your line was he returns with empty arms.

A newborn cries in the cell. The guards jerk awake and run to the king. Kamsa leaps out of bed, the Bhagavata says, hair loose, stumbling, and rushes to the prison. This is the eighth child, the one the voice warned him about at the wedding. Devaki holds the baby close and begs him. It's a girl, a daughter of your own house. Don't kill a girl. You've taken so many of my children. Leave me just this one. Kamsa doesn't hear her. He tears the child out of her arms.
screen: `A CRY IN THE CELL.` → `KAMSA RUNS TO THE PRISON.` → `"IT'S A GIRL. LEAVE ME THIS ONE."`

segments.voice: He swings the baby by the feet to dash her against a stone, and she slips out of his grip. She rises into the air, and she is no longer a baby. The Bhagavata calls her the younger sister of Vishnu: a goddess with eight arms, holding weapons, in garlands and bright clothes, with celestial beings singing her praise. And she speaks down to him. What will you gain by killing me, fool? The one who will kill you has already been born, somewhere else. Stop killing the helpless for nothing. Then she is gone. The text says she came to be worshiped on earth in many places, under many names. Kamsa grabbed the one child who could not be harmed, and the attempt only revealed the truth. The crossing worked. The boy is safe across the river, and now even Kamsa knows it. Then, for a moment, Kamsa breaks. He frees Devaki and Vasudeva from their chains. He apologizes, even weeps, and says that everyone acts under fate, and that he has been cruel. Devaki and Vasudeva forgive him. A gentle moment, from Kamsa of all people. It doesn't last. The next morning his ministers advise that, if the child is out there somewhere, newborns across the land should be hunted. Kamsa agrees. The goddess told him to stop killing the helpless. He heard it, and chose fear anyway.

885.title: Putana
885.hook: a beautiful stranger walks into Nanda's house, smiling, and picks up the baby, and nobody stops her
885.howItsDone: The killing of Putana is told in the Bhagavata Purana's tenth book and is one of the childhood episodes Hindus retell in songs, dance-dramas and temple art about Krishna.

segments.voice: Yesterday the girl slipped from Kamsa's hands as a goddess, and Kamsa, after a moment of remorse, chose fear and sent his people after newborns. Your line was stop killing the helpless for nothing.

Nanda is away in Mathura, paying his dues to the king, and Vasudeva, meeting him there, has warned him: go home quickly, there may be trouble in Gokula. Back in the village, a woman arrives. She is beautiful, the Bhagavata says, with flowers in her hair, a soft smile, a graceful walk. The cowherd women think a goddess has come to visit. She walks straight into Nanda's house, to the bed where the baby is lying.
screen: `NANDA IS AWAY.` → `A BEAUTIFUL STRANGER.` → `SHE WALKS TO THE BABY'S BED.`

segments.voice: Putana is one of Kamsa's killers. The Bhagavata calls her a demoness who goes from town to town killing infants, who can travel through the air and take any shape she likes. Today she has taken the shape of a lovely woman. Here is the first unsettling detail. Yashoda and Rohini are right there. They watch her lift the child, so struck by her beauty and sweetness that they just stand there. The danger doesn't break in. It is welcomed. And the text turns the picture around: Putana takes the child on her lap the way someone picks up a sleeping snake, thinking it is a rope. The danger she doesn't see is the baby. And the child? When she came near, the Bhagavata says, he closed his eyes. The verse doesn't say why; commentators offer more than one reason, perhaps hiding his power, perhaps turning from her cruelty. She offers him her breast, smeared with poison. The baby feeds, but he takes more than milk: he draws her very life out with it. She screams, let go, let go. She thrashes, sweating, eyes rolling, and the earth shakes at her cry. As she dies, her disguise falls away, and she collapses in her true form, so enormous that, the text says, trees are crushed beneath her. On top of that terrible body, the cowherd women find the baby, playing, unafraid. The one who came to feed him poison is undone by the act of feeding.

886.title: Putana
886.hook: the cowherds burn Putana's body, and the smoke that rises smells sweet, like fragrant wood
886.howItsDone: Vaishnava teachers and devotees retell Putana's story as an example of Krishna's grace, and the protective rites the cowherd women perform are described in the Bhagavata alongside the names of Vishnu they recite.

segments.voice: Yesterday Putana came smiling into Nanda's house with poison, and the baby drew her life out as he fed. Your line was danger came with a smile.

The cowherd women snatch the baby off Putana's body and carry him away, shaking. Then they protect him the way they know how. The Bhagavata describes it closely: they wave a cow's tail around him, wash him, mark his body with the dust of cows, and touch his limbs one by one while saying names of Vishnu, asking each name to guard a part of him. Feet. Knees. Belly. Heart. Then Yashoda nurses him to sleep. The danger is over. What the story does next with Putana is the surprise.
screen: `THE WOMEN TAKE THE BABY.` → `A NAME FOR EVERY LIMB.` → `YASHODA NURSES HIM TO SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Nanda comes home from Mathura with the other cowherds and finds a giant body lying across the village. He remembers Vasudeva's warning and is amazed: the man saw it coming. The cowherds cut up the body, pile it on a fire and burn it. And the smoke smells sweet, rising fragrant, the Bhagavata says, like aloe wood. Why would a child-killer's pyre smell like incense? The text gives its own answer: because the child had drunk her milk, her wrongs were burned away. Then the narrator, the sage Shuka, says something astonishing. Putana came to kill. She smeared poison on her breast and offered it to the Lord. Even so, because she offered him milk, she reached the place given to a mother. If even she, who came with murder in mind, was given that, Shuka asks, what of those who offer him love? That is the hinge. The Bhagavata doesn't dwell on punishing her. It dwells on the one thing she did that looked like a mother's act, and treats it as hers. Some Vaishnava teachers read this as a picture of grace: the Lord responds to the offering itself, and his touch transforms even an offering made in bad faith. So the same story holds both: the village's right to guard what it loves with every name it knows, and a mercy wider than anyone there expected.

887.title: the butter thief
887.howItsDone: Krishna as the butter thief is a familiar figure in Hindu devotion: images of the child Krishna with butter in his hand are kept in homes and temples, and on Janmashtami some communities hang pots of curd high up for teams to climb and break.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Putana: she came to the baby with poison, and the text says even she was blessed, because she had fed him like a mother. Your line was even she was blessed.

A group of women stands at Yashoda's door, and they have a list. They are the gopis, the cowherd women of the village. Putana is gone, and now there's a different problem, and he's a toddler. Butter has been disappearing all over the village. Curd too. Milk pots are broken. And every trail leads back to this house. So they come to his mother, half laughing, half fed up, and make their case, item by item.
screen: `WOMEN AT YASHODA'S DOOR.` → `BUTTER IS DISAPPEARING.` → `EVERY TRAIL LEADS HERE.`

segments.voice: Here is their list, as the Bhagavata Purana gives it. He turns the calves loose before milking time, and when someone scolds him, he laughs. He gets into the milk and curd, and when he's had his fill, he feeds the rest to the monkeys. If a monkey won't eat, he breaks the pot. People hang their pots high from the ceiling on ropes, so he drags over stools and a mortar and climbs, or makes a hole in the bottom of the pot and drinks from underneath. In a dark storeroom he doesn't even need a lamp: the jewels he wears light the way. That's the case for the prosecution. Then the turn. All the while, Krishna sits beside his mother with wide, frightened eyes, the picture of a child who has never touched a pot in his life. The women look at that face and can't keep scolding. They laugh. And Yashoda, the text says, smiles and doesn't have the heart to punish him. Notice what kind of complaint this is. Nobody stops making butter. Nobody locks the door. They keep coming to report him, and in the reporting they get to talk about him, and be near him. Some devotional teachers read the stolen butter as the heart of the devotee: the thing you hang up high, out of reach, that he finds a way into anyway. Take it that way or simply as a story about a little boy; either way, the village is full of people who keep leaving the butter out.

888.title: the butter thief
888.howItsDone: Krishna bound by Yashoda's rope is remembered in his name Damodara, and some Vaishnava communities honor this story in the autumn month of Kartika with songs and lamps offered to Damodara.

segments.voice: Yesterday the gopis brought Yashoda their list, and one look at the butter thief's frightened face stopped the scolding. Your line was they can't keep scolding.

Early morning in Nanda's house. The servants are busy elsewhere, and Yashoda is churning curd herself, pulling the rope back and forth around the churning stick, her bangles moving, singing, the text says, about the things her little boy has done. Then the little boy arrives. He's hungry, he wants his mother, and he takes hold of the churning stick so she can't go on. She lifts him into her lap and feeds him. A perfectly quiet scene. It's about to fall apart.
screen: `YASHODA CHURNING, SINGING.` → `HE GRABS THE CHURNING STICK.` → `A QUIET MORNING.`

segments.voice: On the fire, the milk starts to boil over. Yashoda sets Krishna down mid-meal and runs to it. He's furious. He bites his lip, cracks open the pot of curd with a stone, slips into another room and eats butter in secret. Yashoda comes back to a broken pot and no child. She follows the trail and finds him on an upturned mortar, handing butter from the hanging pot to a monkey, glancing around in case anyone sees. She picks up a stick. He jumps down and runs, and she runs after him. The Bhagavata pauses to marvel: the one the yogis can't reach even with their minds is being chased around the yard by his mother. She catches him. He cries and rubs his eyes, smearing them. She drops the stick and decides to tie him to the mortar instead, so he'll stay put. The rope is too short, by two fingers' width. She adds another. Still two fingers short. Every rope in the house, always two fingers short, and the neighbor women laugh, and so does she. She's sweating now, flowers slipping from her hair. Krishna sees how tired his mother is, and then, the text says, he lets himself be tied. Nothing in the universe can hold him. A tired mother's love can, because he allows it. Tradition says this is where one of his names comes from: Damodara, the one with a rope around his waist.

889.howItsDone: The freeing of Kubera's sons, called Yamalarjuna in Sanskrit, the twin arjuna trees, is retold in Krishna devotion as part of the Damodara story, and some images show the child pulling the mortar between two trees.

segments.voice: Yesterday the butter thief let himself be tied, once he saw how tired his mother was. Your line was he lets himself be tied.
screen: `THE BUTTER THIEF.` · `HE LETS HIMSELF BE TIED.`

segments.voice: So there he is, a small boy roped to a heavy wooden mortar, and his mother has gone back to her housework. A child might sulk, or cry. Krishna looks around the yard. Near the house stand two tall arjuna trees, side by side. And the Bhagavata lets us in on something nobody in the village knows: those two trees used to be people. They've been standing there a long time, waiting for this exact boy. Today the mortar goes for a walk.
screen: `TIED TO THE MORTAR.` → `TWO ARJUNA TREES.` → `THEY USED TO BE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The trees were once Nalakuvara and Manigriva, the sons of Kubera, the god of wealth. Proud and drunk, they were playing in a river with a crowd of young women, wearing nothing, when the sage Narada happened by. The women, embarrassed, covered themselves at once. The brothers didn't bother. So Narada cursed them to stand as trees, but his curse came with a way out: they would stand until they saw Krishna, and then be free. A curse, in this telling, that was also a kindness, because what they lacked was humility, and a tree has time to learn it. Now Krishna crawls toward them, dragging the mortar. He squeezes between the trunks. The mortar turns sideways and wedges against them. He pulls, and with a great crack both trees come crashing down. Out step two shining figures. They bow to the child, praise him, ask that their speech, eyes and hands be given to him from now on, and leave. The cowherds come running at the noise. Who did this? The children playing nearby say: Krishna, dragging the mortar. The grown-ups can hardly believe it. Nanda unties his son, smiling. Look back at this week. A baby carried across a flooding river at night. Putana, blessed in spite of herself. A village that can't stay angry at a thief. And a punishment, a boy tied to a mortar, that becomes the way two prisoners go free.
screen: `KUBERA'S SONS, PROUD AND DRUNK.` · `NARADA'S CURSE, WITH A WAY OUT.` · `THE MORTAR WEDGES BETWEEN THEM.` · then, large: `TWO TREES FALL, TWO MEN GO FREE.`

segments.voice: Feel the weight of your body resting down, like something rooted, and bring to mind one thing that has felt like being tied in place lately: a wait, a limit, a delay you didn't choose. Breathe with it and ask quietly whether anything is being freed, or learned, because you're stuck here, and let the question rest if no answer comes. If you pray, you can hold that place in your prayer.
